qt: to the Commission Eva Kaili (NI) Subject:

According to the information contained in the case file of the investigation dubbed by the press as Qatargate, the secret services of several European countries conducted espionage activities with intrusive monitoring of the political activities of several MEPs. In the conclusive report of the Belgian secret services, VSSE, several MEPs that were considered as main suspects were not persecuted or interrogated. According to the 2014 DG IPOL study entitled ‘The immunity of members of European Parliament’, ‘the failure to prosecute other participants in the alleged offence, so that the MEP alone has been criminally charged for a fact involving a plurality of suspects, has also been treated as fumus persecutionis’. In the light of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware that such violations are happening in a country hosting EU institutions?
How can the absolute immunity and independence of MEPs be guaranteed in a country like Belgium where secret services are acting outside EU law?
How can an MEP be protected from fumus persecutionis?
at: (English version) to the Commission Eva Kaili (NI) (7 March 2024) Subject: Violation of parliamentary immunity According to items in the case file of the investigation the press has called ‘Qatargate’, the Belgian authorities and the secret services of several European countries conducted espionage activities to determine possible interference by foreign countries within the EU institutions. In this regard it is worth underlining that: —
The political activity of several MEPs has also been monitored through the illegal use of wire taps.
The Belgian secret services (VSSE) drafted a report confirming that on 9 December 2022 they were spying outside the house of MEP Eva Kaili, although there were no grounds to justify this action.

The Belgian police drafted a report confirming that on 14 November 2022 they entered Parliament facilities in plain clothes in order to attend a committee meeting hearing and report on MEPs’ political positions.
Having regard to the rules regarding the parliamentary immunity: 1.
Is the Commission aware of these facts?

Can the Commission clarify whether secret services and national authorities of the Member States are authorised to enter the EU institution’s facilities undercover and to spy and report on the political positions of MEPs without lifting their immunity?

to the Commission Eva Kaili (NI) (7 March 2024) Subject: Belgium not a safe place for democracy According to the information contained in the case file of the investigation dubbed by the press as Qatargate, the secret services of several European countries conducted espionage activities with intrusive monitoring of the political activities of several MEPs. In the conclusive report of the Belgian secret services, VSSE, several MEPs that were considered as main suspects were not persecuted or interrogated. According to the 2014 DG IPOL study entitled ‘The immunity of members of European Parliament’, ‘the failure to prosecute other participants in the alleged offence, so that the MEP alone has been criminally charged for a fact involving a plurality of suspects, has also been treated as fumus persecutionis’. In the light of the above: 1.
Is the Commission aware that such violations are happening in a country hosting EU institutions?
2. How can the absolute immunity and independence of MEPs be guaranteed in a country like Belgium where secret services are acting outside EU law? 3.
How can an MEP be protected from fumus persecutionis?

Joint answer given by Mr Hahn on behalf of the European Commission (12 July 2024) Given the organisational autonomy of the EU institutions, each institution is responsible for its internal investigations and for ensuring that the protocols regarding the status and the immunity of their members are respected.
Therefore, the Commission is not in a position to make the requested assessment or express any view on this matter. Neither does the Commission comment on national investigations.
